Windowing and STFT¶

Compute the DFT of an "on bin" (integer bin) sinusoid and plot.

In [26]:
N = 128
k = 8

n = np.arange(N)
x = np.cos(2 * np.pi * k * n / N)

X = np.zeros(N)

for m in range(N):
    s = 0
    for n in range(N):
        s += x[n] * np.exp(-1j * 2 * np.pi * m * n / N)
    X[m] = s

plt.figure()
plt.plot(np.abs(X))
plt.title(f"DFT Magnitude (on-bin sinusoid, k={k}, N={N})")
plt.xlabel("Frequency index")
plt.ylabel("Magnitude")
plt.show()

Apply a hanning window to both sinusoids and recompute the DFT and plot.

In [28]:
N = 128
k_on = 8
k_off = 7.5

n = np.arange(N)
x_on  = np.cos(2 * np.pi * k_on  * n / N)
x_off = np.cos(2 * np.pi * k_off * n / N)

# Hanning window
w = 0.5 - 0.5 * np.cos(2 * np.pi * n / (N - 1))
x_on_w  = x_on  * w
x_off_w = x_off * w

def dft(x):
    N = len(x)
    X = np.zeros(N, dtype=complex)
    for m in range(N):
        s = 0
        for nn in range(N):
            s += x[nn] * np.exp(-1j * 2 * np.pi * m * nn / N)
        X[m] = s
    return X

X_on  = dft(x_on_w)
X_off = dft(x_off_w)

plt.figure()
plt.plot(np.abs(X_on),  label='On-bin (windowed)')
plt.plot(np.abs(X_off), label='Off-bin (windowed)')
plt.title("Windowed DFT: On-bin vs Off-bin")
plt.xlabel("Frequency index")
plt.ylabel("Magnitude")
plt.legend()
plt.show()

Apply a blackman harris window to both sinusoids and recompute the DFT and plot.

In [29]:
N = 128
k_on  = 8     # on-bin index (integer)
k_off = 7.5   # off-bin index (non-integer)

n = np.arange(N)
x_on  = np.cos(2 * np.pi * k_on  * n / N)
x_off = np.cos(2 * np.pi * k_off * n / N)


a0, a1, a2, a3 = 0.35875, 0.48829, 0.14128, 0.01168
theta = 2 * np.pi * n / (N - 1)
w = a0 - a1*np.cos(theta) + a2*np.cos(2*theta) - a3*np.cos(3*theta)

x_on_w  = x_on  * w
x_off_w = x_off * w

def dft(x):
    N = len(x)
    X = np.zeros(N, dtype=complex)
    for m in range(N):
        s = 0.0 + 0.0j
        for nn in range(N):
            s += x[nn] * np.exp(-1j * 2 * np.pi * m * nn / N)
        X[m] = s
    return X

X_on  = dft(x_on_w)
X_off = dft(x_off_w)

# -----------------------
# One overlap plot (DFT magnitudes)
# -----------------------
plt.figure()
plt.plot(np.abs(X_on),  label='On-bin (Blackman–Harris)')
plt.plot(np.abs(X_off), label='Off-bin (Blackman–Harris)')
plt.title("Windowed DFT: On-bin vs Off-bin (Blackman–Harris)")
plt.xlabel("Frequency index")
plt.ylabel("Magnitude")
plt.legend()
plt.show()

Describe what happened in all of the above cases. What happened to the frequency resolution, was their leakage, what do the side/main lobes look like?

As you moved from rectangular → Hanning → Blackman–Harris windows, leakage decreased dramatically, sidelobes got smaller and cleaner, and the main lobe widened, reducing frequency resolution but producing a smoother, more accurate amplitude representation of off‑bin frequencies.

Applying the STFT¶

Apply the STFT (use scipy.stft) to one of the files listed below, then graph the spectrogram.

  • 'BobMarley_track1.wav'
  • 'MilesDavis_track2.wav'
  • 'Radiohead_track3.wav'
  • 'TheBlackKeys_track4.wav'

See what happens when you change:

  • the frame size (nperseg)
  • the window type
  • the amount of overlap
  • the amount of padding (nfft)
In [30]:
from scipy.signal import stft

(fs, x) = read("../audio/BobMarley_track1.wav") 

nperseg = 5000
window  = 'hamm'
noverlap = nperseg // 2
nfft = nperseg

f, t, Zxx = stft(x, fs=fs, window=window, nperseg=nperseg, noverlap=noverlap, nfft=nfft)

plt.pcolormesh(t, f, np.abs(Zxx))
plt.title("Spectrogram")
plt.xlabel("Time (s)")
plt.ylabel("Frequency (Hz)")
plt.show()

STFT Pseudo Code¶

For HW3, you will write your own STFT function. To get you started on that process, write out the pseudocode for the STFT. You should expect similar inputs to the scipy.stft function.

FUNCTION STFT(x, nperseg, noverlap, window, nfft):

1. Make the window (length = nperseg)

2. Set hop = nperseg - noverlap

3. For each frame:
      a. Take a chunk of x of length nperseg
      b. Multiply it by the window
      c. Zero‑pad to nfft
      d. Take the FFT of the frame
      e. Store the FFT result as one column

4. Return all FFT columns as the STFT matrix

Bandwidth¶

Look up the function documentation here.

For Track (a) and Track (b), calculate the bandwidth using the spectral_bandwidth function. Compare the change in output for both (a) and (b) using two different FFT sizes in your STFT: one relatively small, and the other relatively large.

Plot your results for each by plotting the normalized audio and normalized feature on top of each other. (You may do this using the frames_to_time function if you wish.) Your graph output should be a 4x4 grid (2 songs, 2 different FFT sizes).

In [31]:
import librosa
import librosa.display

(fs, a) = read('../audio/BobMarley_track1.wav')
(fs2, b) = read('../audio/MilesDavis_track2.wav')

a = a.astype(float)
b = b.astype(float)


fft_small = 1024
fft_large = 4096
hop = 512


bwA_s = librosa.feature.spectral_bandwidth(y=a, sr=fs, n_fft=fft_small, hop_length=hop)
bwA_l = librosa.feature.spectral_bandwidth(y=a, sr=fs, n_fft=fft_large, hop_length=hop)

bwB_s = librosa.feature.spectral_bandwidth(y=b, sr=fs2, n_fft=fft_small, hop_length=hop)
bwB_l = librosa.feature.spectral_bandwidth(y=b, sr=fs2, n_fft=fft_large, hop_length=hop)



tA_wave = np.arange(len(a)) / fs
tB_wave = np.arange(len(b)) / fs2

tA_s = (np.arange(len(bwA_s)) * hop) / fs
tA_l = (np.arange(len(bwA_l)) * hop) / fs
tB_s = (np.arange(len(bwB_s)) * hop) / fs2
tB_l = (np.arange(len(bwB_l)) * hop) / fs2


# Simple normalization
na = a / np.max(np.abs(a))
nb = b / np.max(np.abs(b))


fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(10,6))

# Track A – small FFT
ax[0,0].plot(np.arange(len(a))/fs, na)
ax[0,0].plot(tA_s, bwA_s/np.max(bwA_s))
ax[0,0].set_title("A - n_fft = {}".format(fft_small))

# Track A – large FFT
ax[0,1].plot(np.arange(len(a))/fs, na)
ax[0,1].plot(tA_l, bwA_l/np.max(bwA_l))
ax[0,1].set_title("A - n_fft = {}".format(fft_large))

# Track B – small FFT
ax[1,0].plot(np.arange(len(b))/fs2, nb)
ax[1,0].plot(tB_s, bwB_s/np.max(bwB_s))
ax[1,0].set_title("B - n_fft = {}".format(fft_small))

# Track B – large FFT
ax[1,1].plot(np.arange(len(b))/fs2, nb)
ax[1,1].plot(tB_l, bwB_l/np.max(bwB_l))
ax[1,1].set_title("B - n_fft = {}".format(fft_large))

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Always check the sampling rates - you want to make sure that you are using the same sampling rate when making comparisons. If they are not the same, you will need to downsample the ones that are too high (or, alternatively, downsample all of them so that they are 22.05kHz). One way is to use librosa to read in the files - it has an argument for you to specify the sample rate you want:

In [34]:
# the 'load' package from librosa was already installed 
# note that librosa saves the sample rate and data in the opposite order
(data, fs) = load('../audio/BobMarley_track1.wav', sr=44100)#note that 22050 is the default for the "load" function
print(fs, data.shape)

44100 (1322922,)

The other way is via the signal.resample function from scipy. Be careful if you choose to do it this way since the sample rate you saved when loading is no longer the correct sample rate. When the sample rate is 96kHz, it's a bit tricky this way:

In [ ]:
#First, read in as usual:
(fs, a) = read('../uploaded_files/BobMarley_track1.wav')
#Then, downsample:
#size of original in s:
t = a.size/fs
#length of samples you would have with 44.1kHz (desired) sample rate:
newl = int(np.ceil(t*44100)) #must be integer number of samples
ads = signal.resample(a, newl).astype(float) #signal to resample, total samples in new output 
print(ads.shape)
